newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana opens Oil and Gas Africa 1997 conference.
newsitem.headline: Ghana opens Oil and Gas Africa 1997 conference.

text.p: Ghana's President Jerry Rawlings opened a three day oil and gas sector in Accra on Wednesday calling for better use of flared gas as a way to raise living standards.

"Trillions of feet of gas are flared (while) people have no light to study, no gas to cook," he said on the first day of Oil and Gas Africa 1997. "I am glad that the theme of this conference is "Meeting Africa's Growing Oil and Gas needs."

Early talks focused on a proposed West Africa Off-Shore Natural Gas Pipeline to supply five West African countries with a total of 280 million cubic feet/day of eastern Nigerian natural gas from Escravos.
Gas supply contracts for a new 200 MW Ghanaian power plant at Takoradi in eastern Ghana were also under discussion.
Nigeria flares up to 75 percent of gas associated with its oil reserves. A proposed regional pipeline would take gas to Ghana, Ivory Coast, Benin and Togo as well as the rest of Nigeria.
In February, Nigeria signed a letter of intent to supply natural gas to Ghana via a pipeline through Benin and Togo.

The letter covered an agreement between Chevron Corp and Ghana National Petroleum for supplying gas to a new Volta River Authority thermal power plant at Takoradi in eastern Ghana due on stream in 1997.
The Takoradi plant would inititally be fired with Nigerian crude oil and later switch to using around 30 million cubic feet/day of natural gas.
But Chevron faces increasing competition from other interested gas suppliers.
U.S.-based United Meridian International Corp (UMIC) has also expressed interest in building pipelines to supply the Takoradi plant using expanding supplies from Ivory Coast.

"We can have gas in Takoradi in 18 months. Building a pipeline from Nigeria will take 2 - 5 years," Damien de Gheldere, Vice-President Administration of UMIC Cote d'Ivoire, told Reuters at the sidelines of the conference.
A shorter 200 km pipeline would be needed from Ivory Coast's Kudu field compared to 640 km from Nigeria's Escravos field.
Ivory Coast signed two separate offshore gas production contracts last week, with UMIC and Houston-based Apache Corp, and is keen to develop electricity and gas export markets in Ghana.

"Chevron needs to accelerate its market plan. Getting the pipeline in place by 2003 or even 2005 might be too late," said Steven Hill, Vice-President of Europe-based power group ABB Asea Brown Boveri Group.

"There will be competing sources of gas in the region, from UMIC and Apache in Cote d'Ivoire, Addax in Benin and the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation, whose Tano Fields look very promising," he added.
Ivory Coast's Minister of Mines and Energy, Mohammed Lamine Fadika, discussed Ivory Coast's plans with Rawlings before a project map at UMIC's display stand. "It is the logical thing to do," he said.
Shell Nigeria has proposed a third option of an overland pipeline - an option favoured by Nigeria's National Gas Corporation, said Hill.
"We see a landline as an unacceptable investment risk. It can be sabotaged, one will have to pay all sorts of royalties, taxes, right-of-ways," he said.
